Up to 100% of men have microplastics in their semen

I got mine to zero. The first documented case.

A 2024 study detected microplastics in 100% of human and dog testicular tissue.

If you haven't slept enough, should you still exercise?

It depends.

If you're severely sleep deprived, dial back the intensity and prioritize recovery. However, the occasional bad night doesn't automatically mean you should skip exercise. In fact, exercise helps with part of the metabolic disruption that follows acute sleep deprivation.

Observationally, short sleep (less than 6 hours/night) is associated with higher mortality in people falling short of physical activity guidelines, but among those meeting the guidelines, that excess risk is absent or diminished.

I'm not saying that exercise cancels out insufficient sleep. But the data suggest staying active may buffer some of its consequences.

From my last appearance on @hubermanlab.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick on a question plenty of us ask: slept badly, should I still train?

Her answer: it depends. If you're really wrecked, ease off the intensity and look after recovery. But one rough night isn't a reason to skip it. Exercise actually helps with some of the damage a short night does to your metabolism.

She points out short sleepers who stay active don't carry the same extra risk as short sleepers who don't move.

It doesn't cancel out bad sleep. But it helps. Go lighter, but still go.

Breast cancer cells are LOADED with insulin receptors. That's important to know for preventing/treating it. Why? Read on...

In 159 breast tumors, insulin receptor content was more than 6 times higher than in normal breast tissue. And the receptors worked: they bound insulin and switched on.

Many cancer cells favor a form of the insulin receptor (IR-A) that acts mainly as a growth signal, not a sugar-handling one. Insulin tells these cells to grow.

512 women with early breast cancer had fasting insulin checked. Highest vs lowest quarter: 2x the distant recurrence, 3.1x the death rate.

Few doctors check fasting insulin. Fewer still know that Low-carb/Keto/Carnivore is the most direct way to bring it down. I've made videos on this (see below).

If high insulin goes with more breast cancer AND worse outcomes, why isn't fasting insulin part of every breast cancer workup?

Studies and my videos below...

A few years back, researchers at the Cleveland Clinic pulled the records of more than 122,000 people who’d walked onto a treadmill and pushed until they couldn’t. They weren’t looking for personal bests. They were looking for something simpler: how long those people lived afterward.

They sorted everyone by how fit they were for their age and sex — from the least fit all the way up to the rare ones who landed two standard deviations above average. Then they watched what happened over the next eight-plus years.

The pattern was blunt. The fitter people were, the longer they tended to live. And the line never flattened. The people at the very top of the fitness charts still had lower mortality than the people who were merely “highly fit.” Even past age 70. Even with high blood pressure. No plateau. No penalty for being elite.

Low fitness carried roughly the same extra risk as smoking or diabetes. Elite fitness didn’t just erase that risk — it kept lowering it further. The authors wrote the sentence that still gets quoted: there was “no observed upper limit of benefit.”

Most of the headlines about exercise talk about minutes per week and sweet spots. This one measured what your body could actually do. The people who could do more, on that treadmill, lived longer. The data didn’t find a ceiling.

Sometimes the simplest message is the one that holds up: get fitter. Then get fitter again. The treadmill doesn’t seem to care how fit you already are.

In a quiet laboratory above the streets of Zagreb, Dr. Andrija Karačić stared at a set of bacterial profiles that refused to match the textbook.

Karačić, a Croatian physician who trained in abdominal surgery and later founded the country’s first dedicated Gut Microbiome Center (Centar za crijevni mikrobiom), had spent years studying how diet reshapes the trillions of microbes living in the human intestine. Like most of the field, he had absorbed the near-universal claim: remove plants and their fiber, and the microbiome collapses. Diversity plummets. Beneficial fiber-fermenting bacteria vanish. 

Pathological shifts follow. The carnivore diet—strictly animal foods, zero plants—should have been the perfect experiment to confirm that prediction.

In 2024 his team finally found a subject willing to be tested. The man was 32, healthy, physically active, and had eaten nothing but meat, eggs, butter, cream, and hard cheeses for four full years. No vegetables. No fruit. No grains. No legumes. He reported better skin, better digestion, and no health complaints. His bloodwork and body composition looked unremarkable for a lean, training man.

When the 16S sequencing results arrived from the partner lab in Germany, Karačić and his colleagues expected a barren landscape. What they saw instead was a microbiome dominated by Firmicutes and populated by genera classically labeled as fiber degraders: Faecalibacterium, Blautia, various Lachnospiraceae, Bacteroides, and Roseburia. Alpha and beta diversity matched carefully selected healthy omnivore controls of similar age, sex, and lifestyle. Predicted functional capacity was comparable. The carnivore’s profile was actually least similar to people who ate meat every day as part of a conventional mixed diet. 

The paper, titled “The gut microbiome without any plant food? A case study on the gut microbiome of a healthy carnivore,” became the first published long-term look at the topic. The authors were careful: one person is not a population, and elevated Escherichia and Salmonella sequences raised questions. Still, the central observation was hard to ignore. A man who had consumed essentially zero dietary fiber for years had not developed an obviously pathological, collapsed microbiome.

Karačić’s group kept looking. By 2026 they had assembled ten healthy adults who had stayed on a carnivore diet for an average of roughly three years (range extending beyond five). These were compared against 874 confounder-matched omnivore controls. Alpha-diversity was not reduced; the carnivores showed higher Chao1 richness, indicating more low-abundance taxa. There were no significant losses of Akkermansia muciniphila, the Lactobacillus group, or butyrate-related pathways. 

Taxonomic shifts appeared—enrichment of certain low-abundance phyla such as Synergistetes and Desulfobacterota, reductions in some Bifidobacterium and specific Faecalibacterium and Roseburia species—but multivariate models showed the diet itself, not age, BMI, sleep, or place of residence, was the dominant driver. 
Functional profiling told a more nuanced story. 

The carnivore microbiomes were enriched for amino-acid degradation, B-vitamin synthesis, energy metabolism, and protein fermentation. Some modules linked to cytotoxicity, inflammation, and constipation were also elevated. The authors noted potential long-term risks while emphasizing that the findings challenged the assumption that dietary fiber is required to maintain microbial diversity. They suggested certain animal-derived nutrients might exert previously under-appreciated prebiotic-like effects.

The work did not declare the carnivore diet universally safe or optimal. It did not claim the microbiome was identical to that of a fiber-rich eater. What it did was document, in healthy people living the diet for years rather than days, that the predicted pathological collapse had not occurred. The gut ecosystem had adapted

In the spring of 1961, at Trenton State Hospital in New Jersey, a nurse pushed a needle into the arm of a 32-year-old mathematician and watched the clock.

John Nash—already famous for game theory, already slipping into the private universe of voices and conspiracies that would later make him the subject of A Beautiful Mind—had been transferred to the insulin unit. 

His Princeton colleagues had begged the hospital to put him there. It was better staffed than the regular wards. It was also the best treatment medicine had for schizophrenia.

Every morning, large doses of insulin drove his blood sugar so low that his brain shut down. He slipped into coma. His body stiffened. Sometimes he seized. Staff waited roughly an hour, then brought him back with a glucose solution, often through a tube. Day after day. Week after week. Six weeks in all.

Nash later called it torture. He remembered the surrounding rituals—the showers afterward, the sugar water, the group of other patients—but almost nothing of the coma itself. The treatment carved gaps in his memory. He resented it for years; on letters he sometimes listed his return address as “Insulin Institute.” During those weeks he also became a vegetarian, he later said, partly as a quiet protest against what he saw as cruelty.

The theory, developed by Austrian psychiatrist Manfred Sakel in the 1920s and 1930s, was that starving the brain of glucose would somehow jolt or “reset” psychotic thinking. Hospitals built special units. Patients were chosen carefully—those with recent onset and better odds. Reported success rates varied wildly; some doctors claimed dramatic recoveries, while critics noted that patients already likely to improve were selected and given intensive attention. Mortality ran roughly 1–5 percent. 

Permanent brain damage was a recognized risk. One contemporary study even suggested certain forms of brain damage were therapeutic because they reduced “tension and hostility.”

By the late 1950s the evidence was collapsing. A controlled trial found no difference between insulin comas and comas induced by barbiturates. Chlorpromazine and other antipsychotics proved safer and more practical. Within a decade the insulin units emptied.

Nash eventually stabilized enough to return to mathematics, though his recovery was long, uneven, and not simply a triumph of the treatment. He continued to struggle for years. Many others were not so fortunate. Singer-songwriter Townes Van Zandt, treated as a teenager in Galveston, lost large stretches of long-term memory; his mother later called allowing the therapy her biggest regret. 

Psychiatric survivor Leonard Roy Frank described dozens of forced insulin comas as “the most devastating, painful and humiliating experience of my life.”
Insulin coma therapy was not fringe quackery. For two decades it was mainstream, labor-intensive, and sincerely believed. It gave desperate doctors something concrete to do in an era when schizophrenia often meant lifelong institutionalization. 

It also left scars—literal and figurative—that patients carried long after the last insulin unit closed.

The mathematician’s mind eventually found its way back. The method that tried to force the journey never did.

Mike Archer stood at the edge of the wheat field as the last of the light drained out of the sky, notebook open, boots sunk a little in the loose soil. The numbers had been circling in his head for weeks, and now they were settling into something that felt unavoidable.

He had spent years around bones—fossil ones, mostly—reading the long record of life and death written into rock. Living animals were different. These were the ones still running around under the grain.

Every few years the mice arrived in force. Not a scattering, but a plague: hundreds to a thousand per hectare in the worst seasons, dense enough that you could hear the rustle when you walked the rows. Farmers poisoned them. 

There was little choice; the grain would otherwise vanish into the burrows. Archer had pulled the figures together from the CSIRO data and the plague records. Average it out, account for the four-year cycle, the fraction of land baited, the kill rate once the baits went down. It came to something on the order of a hundred mice dead per hectare each year just to keep the wheat growing.

He did the protein math next, because that was the only fair comparison. A hectare of wheat, average yield, usable protein fraction. Then the same exercise for a steer raised on the rangelands that would not grow crops anyway—native grasses, sparse cover, one animal delivering a carcass that translated into tens of kilograms of protein. Two animals, maybe a couple more when you counted the occasional losses, for every hundred kilos of usable protein from the cattle. Fifty-odd mice for the same amount from the grain.

He closed the notebook. The ratio sat there, stubborn: roughly twenty-five times more sentient deaths on the grain side, at least under Australian conditions and the numbers he could defend. It was not a defense of every feedlot or every industrial barn. It was narrower than that—rangeland cattle versus the mice that died so the vegetarian plate could stay free of them. Still, it inverted the usual story.

Archer walked back toward the vehicle. The field looked empty now, the grain cut, the stubble pale. Somewhere under it, or already scavenged, were the mice that had not made it through the season. He had no particular fondness for the argument he was about to make public. It complicated things people preferred simple. In the colonial and early American period, American lobster was abundant, highly perishable, and labor-intensive to prepare. Near the New England coast it carried low status: gathered by hand, sometimes used as fertilizer or bait, and eaten mainly by people with limited choices. 

The familiar stories of prisoners or servants complaining about being fed lobster too often (or of laws/contracts capping it at two or three times a week) are later folklore—identical in structure to earlier 19th-century tales told about salmon, and unsupported by primary colonial records. Prison diets of the era were typically salt pork, beans, bread, and salt cod. 

Still, the broader point holds: lobster was cheap coastal subsistence food, not a delicacy. William Bradford’s 1622–23 remark that the best the Plymouth settlers could offer was a lobster or fish with water is best read as a comment on scarcity and the absence of proper meat and bread, not pure contempt for the crustacean itself.

By the late 19th and early 20th centuries the status had flipped. Canning, railroads that carried live or packed lobster inland to diners who had never known the coastal stigma, tourism, and better cooking methods turned it into a luxury item. What had once been plentiful and low-prestige became scarce and high-priced.

Against that backdrop, the modern death-row last-meal tradition produces an irony. On July 8, 1999, Allen Lee Davis—convicted of the 1982 murders of a pregnant woman and her two young daughters in Jacksonville, Florida—was executed by electric chair at Florida State Prison. For his final meal he requested and received one lobster tail, fried potatoes, a half-pound of fried shrimp, six ounces of fried clams, half a loaf of garlic bread, and 32 ounces of A&W Root Beer. 

A large man (around 350 pounds), he ate a spread that would have been unremarkable luxury fare by the late 20th century and that would have been almost unimaginable as “poor food” two or three centuries earlier.

Davis’s request is one of several documented cases in which condemned inmates specifically asked for lobster (or lobster with steak, shrimp, etc.). In the historical frame, it closes a long arc: the same animal once associated with abundance, low status, and (in folklore) institutional punishment had become a final, deliberate indulgence—the opposite of the colonial stereotype. 

The transformation was driven less by any change in the lobster itself than by technology, markets, and shifting cultural valuation.

hits.text: A bad night of sleep matters more for metabolism than most people think, but movement can offset a lot of it. A single night of 4 hours of sleep cut insulin sensitivity by about 25% in healthy adults, in both the liver and muscle. outsiders.name: @levelsio
outsiders.text:
It’s been a few months now testing the @maticrobots vacuum cleaner

Before we had a Roborock (essentially a Roomba knockoff)

But the Roborock became kinda useless, it'd always get stuck in any type of cable, it'd always get stuck not being able to get on to the thick rug, so you'd have to prep the room every single time just to use it

Too much work so we just stopped using it

The Matic is, well, completely different. It's not flat or low, it's a chunky tall kinda cute looking cube shaped thing with 2 big wheels

And it's a different philosophy, it has cameras and tries to understand its environment, more like a modern robot or a self driving Tesla than a classic Roomba-type vacuum

That makes it just way way better, it doesn't get stuck in cables, it doesn't get stuck in rugs, it drives and turns around the room almost like a mini car

It's also way more silent than Roborock or Roomba-type vacuums, and measurably way more powerful in both vacuuming and mopping

They also respond very fast to feedback and improve things fast, like companies should be these days (instead of getting stuck in some hellish corporate support flow)

Another thing, I don't trust consumer devices connected to the internet (and nor should you) so of course I asked to Claude to analyze if it was phoning home (remember the other vacuums who upload your house plan to China, that was true). Claude was conclusive, Matic never phoned home anything, excellent

Maybe the best part is, it just looks cute and you wanna anthropomorphize it, and they include 2 googly eye stickers so it becomes even more like a dog/cat/pet

@mehul made a great thing!
